name: NSE: box registration, sign-on, and the order lifecycle over NNF

steps.comment: NNF field maps are private tag numbers, which is less readable than a FIX scenario and deliberate: a scenario states what goes on the wire, and a friendlier vocabulary would hide exactly the details these tests exist to pin. Every step says what it is doing instead. 35=transaction code, 9003=UserId, 9004=ErrorCode, 9170=BoxId, 9120=BrokerId, 9140=sign-on UserId, 55/9100=Symbol/Series, 9110=BookType, 54=BuySell, 38=Volume, 44=Price, 37=OrderNumber, 151=LeavesQty, 14=CumQty, 9204=Day flag, 9123=Pro/Client, 1=ClientAccount.
There is no one-message logon here. A connection is a box: it registers, the box signs on, and only then may a user sign on over it.
The registration response is the bare 40-byte header: it carries no Box ID, because the structure has no room for one.
SIGN_ON_REQUEST_IN. The password is not verified -- a simulator holds no credential store -- but it is struck out of the audit.

The market's state is asked for, never volunteered: SYSTEM_INFORMATION_IN once signed on. A real client sets its streams up from the answer and asserts on a second one, so sign-on itself sends nothing more.
A fresh Regular Lot buy. NSE has no ClOrdID: the confirmation is where the client learns the OrderNumber, and it is the only handle it gets.
Amend it. The request names the exchange's own order number, because there is nothing else to name it by.
Cancel it, by the same number.
Cancelling it again is refused: NNF answers with the erroring form of the same transaction, carrying a numeric code, because it has no session-level Reject at all. 16013 is ERR_INVALID_ORDER_NUMBER.
